items.excerpt: WASHINGTON Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Thursday, including US President Donald Trump defending the Iran war amid midterm losses, world leaders offering mixed reactions to Democrats' victory in US midterm elections, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps saying two oil tankers and a tugboat catching fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. US President Donald Trump said the war in Iran was worth the political and economic costs as his Republic Party lost the midterm elections, insisting that the country had "no choice" but to take military action to prevent Tehran from obtaining nuclear weapons. Asked at the White House whether he believed the conflict was worth it, Trump responded: “I do. Yeah. I mean, well, you have no choice.” “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” he added. Asked about Vice President JD Vance's suggestion that the war in Iran contributed to Republican losses, Trump agreed, acknowledging that the conflict had pushed gasoline prices higher in the short term. “Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up,” he said. Meanwhile Vance blamed the war with Iran for Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections, saying voter anger over the conflict drove former Trump supporters to back Democrats. ... World leaders on Wednesday offered mixed reactions to Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections, with some welcoming the outcome as a sign of political change while others reaffirming their commitment to maintaining strong relations with Washington. Democrats secured control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's elections, delivering a major setback to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. German Defense Minister ... Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Thursday said that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz after vessels attempted to use what it called an unauthorized route. In a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency, the Revolutionary Guard said a large oil tanker struck a mine Wednesday night while attempting to pass through an “unauthorized route” south of the strait. The tanker caught fire and came to a halt, the statement said. In a separate incident, another supertanker caught fire while leaving the route in the eastern part of the strait, it said. A tugboat approaching to help extinguish the blaze also caught fire, the statement added.

items.excerpt: After midterm loss, Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war that contributed to GOP debacle WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump faces a tough decision on his unpopular war against Iran after the Republican Party's midterm losses. He had hinted at escalating the conflict if Tehran didn't meet his terms by Election Day. Now with the election behind him, Trump must decide whether to escalate, maintain the status quo or find a pathway out of the conflict. Despite acknowledging the political cost, Trump on Wednesday said his decision to launch the conflict was the right one. The war has caused significant casualties and had an economic impact around the globe. The AP Voter Poll found about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to shaping how they voted for Congress. Inflation, tariffs and a voter revolt: The midterm verdict on Trump's economy WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump was publicly humbled by inflation in Tuesday’s midterm elections, as public anger over rising prices caused a blistering set of losses for Republicans. Most voters said that Trump’s own policies had smothered growth and drove costs even higher, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. The president’s message that the fault lay with his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, didn’t land. About two-thirds of voters said inflation was more because of Trump’s policies. Democratic victories in Tuesday’s midterms signaled that most voters don’t believe the economy or Trump is working for them. Arab parties extend a hand to try to topple Netanyahu but challenges remain TAYIBE, Israel (AP) — A veteran Arab lawmaker in Israel says his bloc is willing to break with decades of precedent and join forces with Jewish-led parties in a shared bid to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long rule. But any such partnership could be politically fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israel’s wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Netanyahu’s opponents, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticize Israel's policies, but reject its identity as a Jewish state.

items.title: The Federal Reserve's Initial November Inflation Forecast Has Arrived, and Things Are Getting Downright Ugly for Wall Street | The Motley Fool
items.excerpt: By Sean Williams – Nov 5, 2026 at 4:06AM EST ... ## Uh-Oh! Inflation appears to be reaccelerating. Though there's no perfect inflation prediction tool, the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's Inflation Nowcasting tool does an exceptional job of accounting for new economic data and adjusting inflation forecasts in real time. On Nov. 2, Wall Street got its first look at the initial November inflation forecast and the latest update on the October figures. The broad-based Consumer Price Index (CPI) is projected to creep slightly higher to 3.74% in October, before exploding to an annualized 4.25% in November. But what's even more unnerving is the expected jump in Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) and Core PCE – the latter excludes volatile food and energy costs. PCE is the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge. ... The Cleveland Fed's Inflation Nowcasting tool predicts PCE will jump from a reported 3.6% in September to 3.77% in October and 4.03% in November. Meanwhile, Core PCE is expected to trudge higher from a reported 3.1% in September to 3.2% in October and 3.31% in November. In other words, Trumpflation (inflation driven by President Donald Trump's policies) appears to be worsening, which is terrible news for the stock market.

items.title: Oil falls for a fourth day on expectations for lower risk of Iran war escalation
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Nov 5 2026 12:02 AM EST Updated 14 Min Ago Oil prices fell for a fourth day on Thursday on expectations the losses U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered in Congressional elections this week may reduce the risk of further escalation of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Todd Korol | Reuters Brent crude futures edged up on Thursday as investors weighed the future course of the US-Israeli war with Iran after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered heavy losses in midterm elections this week. Brent futures were up $1.53, or ⁠1.6%, at $96.15 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 52 cents, or 0.6%, to $88.64. "The situation in the Middle ​East is still unresolved and that's why ​there is some modest recovery ​in prices at the moment," said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at UBS. Brent is more impacted by geopolitical factors, while WTI is a domestic US benchmark, Staunovo said. Both tumbled by more than 8% in the previous session to settle at their lowest since August 31. The ⁠conflict ‌with Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel in February, and the ⁠resulting higher fuel prices for US consumers were major grievances for voters in Tuesday's rout of Republicans. "Markets are assessing the impact of the midterm elections on Donald Trump's next steps with the Iran war, pricing in more likelihood for the war to end," said June Goh, senior oil analyst at ‌Sparta Commodities. "However, there will be more volatility ahead as the path to full diplomacy to end the war is still wrought with many unknowns while the global strategic reserves have drawn very thin," she said. Uncertainty ​remains before the new Democratic-controlled Congress takes office in January, analysts said. Citi said in a note there were concerns that with the midterms over, the White House could focus on its executive powers in foreign policy and potentially escalate conflict with Iran. Eurasia Group lowered its estimate for the chance of renewed US strikes on Iran ⁠to 60% from 65%, but also cut the probability of a deal to 10% from 20%, as Iran has held firm on its ‌demands and Trump was unlikely to accept terms seen as a defeat. It raised ‌the likelihood of a continued standoff to 30% from 15%. Despite the recent drop in oil prices, escalation is likely to produce a sharper increase into a band of $110 to $125 per barrel for Brent, Eurasia Group said in a note.

items.title: Democrats vow to rein in Trump as he shows off White House ballroom By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Democrats vowed to use their resounding midterm victory to rein in President Donald Trump, setting up two years of possible deadlock in Washington, as Trump spent his first post-election appearance showing off his under-construction White House ballroom. A wave of anger over Trump’s policies, particularly the US-Iran war’s role in pushing the cost of living higher, helped Democrats take the Senate, where they flipped seats in deeply Republican states for a majority of at least 54-44. Democrats also gained at least 30 seats in the House of Representatives. It will be the first time that Trump, a Republican who also held the White House from 2017 to 2021, has had to contend with Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Wednesday that the incoming majority would be focused on affordability and accountability. "We don’t work for Donald Trump," Jeffries, a New York lawmaker who is on track to become the first Black speaker of the House, told reporters on Wednesday. "We work for the American people. And the days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over." ... He turned only briefly to the elections during his nearly hour-long appearance, telling reporters, "I’ll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto." Trump had cast the midterm elections as a referendum on the first half of his second four-year stint in the White House, repeatedly urging his Republican base to "pretend I’m on the ballot," a message that Democratic Party leaders were happy to amplify. The result: voters in conservative strongholds who propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at Trump’s stewardship of the country. In Texas, the biggest Republican-led state before Tuesday, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning their first Senate seat there since 1988 and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate. WAITING ON ALASKA, MISSISSIPPI Extremely close Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi remained uncalled as of Wednesday, leaving open the possibility that the Democrats’ majority could increase by two more seats to 56-44. The Alaska race may not be called for more than a week because of ranked-choice tabulation, while the timeline for a decision in Mississippi remained unclear. Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump’s nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise. The Democratic victory is fueling questions about the longevity of the Supreme Court’s two eldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, and the durability of its ​conservative majority. In the meantime, Republicans hold the reins and will have at least one must-pass piece of legislation ahead – a measure to fund the federal government past December – that they could use to enact conservative priorities during the so-called lame-duck period. The loss also upended Republicans’ House leadership, with House Speaker Mike Johnson saying he would not continue to lead his caucus next year. Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, acknowledged the war with Iran had played a role in his party’s losses but stood by his decision.

items.title: A blue tsunami led by Black voters washes over the South : NPR
items.excerpt: Tuesday's dramatic midterm results have transformed the electoral map, ensuring the future path to power for Democrats and Republicans alike must run through the South. Black voter turnout surged in states like Louisiana and Georgia, as Democrats flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Mississippi is too close to call. Republican-led efforts to redraw House districts to gain more favorable districts in places like Alabama, North Carolina, Texas and Florida backfired, with Democrats poised to net several seats in the region. In several states, the margins at the top of the ticket were so large that the blue tsunami carried down ballot races along with it, flipping several state legislative chambers and statewide offices along the way. Even in contests where Democrats ultimately did not prevail, the millions of dollars of investment from both sides and the wide-ranging repudiation of the Trump administration from every demographic group highlight the South's important role in control of Congress and the White House in future election cycles. ... items.title: Exclusive: First Look at John Lithgow in GIANT Ahead of Cinema Release
items.excerpt: The Tony and Olivier Award-winning play will be screened in more than 900 cinemas across 18 countries beginning November 19. By: A.A. Cristi Nov. 05, 2026 ... An exclusive clip from the cinema release of Mark Rosenblatt’s critically acclaimed debut play GIANT directed by Nicholas Hytner and designed by Bob Crowley, has been released today. Produced by Brian and Dayna Lee, Stephanie Kramer and Nicole Kramer, Josh Fiedler and Robyn Goodman, and Royal Court Theatre in partnership with Trafalgar Releasing, the global leader in Event Cinema distribution, GIANT will be screened in more than 900 cinemas across 18 countries including the United Kingdom, USA, Canada, Australia and select international territories from 19 November 2026. For more information and to buy tickets visit GiantInCinemas.com. Filmed live at the Harold Pinter Theatre in London, the cinema release features the original West End cast comprised of John Lithgow in his Olivier and Tony Award-winning role as Roald Dahl, Olivier Award Winner Elliot Levey as Tom Maschler, Tony Award Nominee Aya Cash as Jessie Stone, Olivier Award Nominee Rachael Stirling as Felicity Dahl, Tessa Bonham Jones as Hallie and Richard Hope as Wally. The production which won three Olivier Awards – Best Actor (John Lithgow), Best Supporting Actor (Elliot Levey) and Best New Play – features lighting design by Anna Watson, sound design by Alexandra Faye Braithwaite and Casting by Arthur Carrington.
